I.

Recommendation/Observations
 
7.6       The Committee was informed that the honorarium for the Education Volunteers is very less.  The Committee
recommends that keeping the conditions peculiar to the North Eastern States in view, the amount of this honorarium must
be increased suitably.
 
Action Taken
 
Regarding Honorarium of Education Volunteer: The Ministry of Human Resource Development, Govt. of India has
already approved for enhancement of honorarium for Education Volunteers engaged in EGS intervention. Accordingly,
financial provision has been kept in draft AWP&B 2007-08.
In the framework of SSA programme, amendment has already been made on 4.1.2007 in which limit of honorarium for
education volunteers have been revised upto Rs.2500 per month.
 
Recommendation/Observations
 
7.11     Some of the States have submitted before the Committee that there is no provision for teacher of vernacular
languages. They have opined that teaching in vernacular languages is helping enrolment as well as retention of children in
the schools. The Committee, therefore, recommends that Government of India may suitably amend the SSA guidelines to
enable the North Eastern States to appoint teachers in vernacular languages also.
 
Action Taken
 
“The SSA programme allows one teacher for every 40 children and at least two teachers for primary school and one
teacher each for every class/grade for upper primary school. These teacher can be used for teaching vernacular language
also”.
SSA, Assam agrees to the recommendation of the Committee for amending the SSA guidelines to enable the North Eastern
States to appoint teachers in vernacular languages also.
 
X.        IMPLEMENTATION OF ICDS IN NORTH EASTERN STATES
 
Recommendation/Observations
 
10.5.3  The Committee also noticed that timely utilization of funds was hampered due to the long financial process
involved in sanction, release etc. of funds.  Encashment permission required by the State also causes some delay in this
regard. In the case of ICDS, it was suggested that the States might be exempted from this permission to allow them direct
access to allotted funds for speedy implementation of the Scheme. 
 
Action Taken
 
The Ministry of Women and Child Development releases funds for implementation of Centrally sponsored ICDS Scheme
to States in accordance with the procedure laid down by the Ministry of Finance.  There is no delay in release of funds by
the Government of India.  As regards procedural formalities for prompt release of funds by the State Govt. to the

11.1     Most of the representatives of the North Eastern States submitted before the Committee that they lacked in

2.5       Teacher Training
 
Recommendation/Observations
 
2.5.5    The Committee also feels that due to the peculiar political, economic, geographical, climatic and other situations
that are specific to J&K, the Government of India needs to revise norms/guidelines for many of its programmes like SSA
& MDM with a view to making them more suitable and relevant.  For instance, the schools in Kashmir region are closed
during the peak winter season.  Whereas, the Government of India is releasing the funds for SSA and other schemes
towards the end of the year.  This results in underutilization or non utilization of funds in certain cases.  In view of poor
economic situation in the State as also due to militancy and other reasons, the proposed pattern of funding for SSA must be
reviewed with a view to providing more funds to the State.
 
Action Taken
 
A Sub-group of SSA Working group on XIth Plan has gone into details on requirement and thrust areas to be covered
under the programme during the XIth Plan.  This group has also suggested revised norms & guidelines for many aspects
covered under SSA programme.  The report of the working group is under consideration of Planning Commission.  As
soon as Planning Commission takes a final view in the matter, action will be taken to notify the revised norms/guidelines
after having them approved by the competent authority.
Food Grains allocation under the Mid Day Meal Programme is generally made in March /April for each ensuing year.
State Governments lift the food grains from FCI godowns on monthly/ quarterly basis depending upon their administrative
convenience and in accordance with their academic calendar.
Central assistance towards cooking cost is also quantified and approved by Mid Day Meal Programme Approval Board
(PAB) after considering the Annual Work Plan & Budget of States/UTs. Funds are released in two equal installments after
deducting unspent balances with the States.
In J&K foodgrains allocation and cooking cost was released on the basis of  school working days (212 days in 2005-06
and 231 days in 2006-07).  State Governments are free to utilize the foodgrains and cooking costs as per their own
academic calendar.

Recommendation/Observations
 
2.5.10  It was suggested to the Committee that the funds for this purpose must be non-lapsable and building work may be
allowed when the winter was over.  The building-plans may be permitted to be approved at the district level according to
the requirements of the area.  The Committee would like to have response of the Department in this regard.
 
Action Taken
 
Unit cost of civil works, like primary/ upper primary schools, classrooms etc. are decided by the State government
concerned and not by the Government of India. State Governments are free to notify different unit costs for different
topographical areas in the state. The J&K Government has been informed of this flexibility. The Secretary (SE&L),
Government of India took a meeting with state government officials and Leh / Kargil SSA  functionaries on 18-19 July,
2007 at Leh in which this point has been further clarified.
 
Recommendation/Observations
 
2.5.11  The Committee during its on-the-spot-visits found that upkeep and basic infrastructure/amenities in the primary
schools needed special attention. Similarly, participation of village education/ school management Committees was
conspicuous by its absence. It needed to be strengthened in a big way as it is the prime mover of the SSA. Toilets in this
region were virtually non-existent in many schools visited by the Committee. Wherever toilets were, they were common
and in a very bad shape. These components need special and urgent-attention by the State Government.
 
Action Taken
 
Upto 2005-06, 4448 toilets have been provided under SSA to J&K. Also State has been advised to converge with the Total
Sanitation Programme and the Drinking Water Mission to provide drinking water & toilet facilities in schools.
 
Recommendation/Observations
 
2.5.12  The Committee notes the progress of SSA in J&K with satisfaction as regards allocating State’s share, increasing
enrolment as well as reducing out-of-the school children gradually. However, the State did not seem to have district-wise
data regarding dropouts from the schools. The Committee feels that districts like Poonch, Rajauri, Doda, Kargil and
Budgam need special  attention which have higher ratio of out-of-school children. Focused attention is required for
education of ST girls belonging to Bakerwal, Gujar and Gaddi tribes. The problem of child labour in carpet weaving and
paper making industry in some districts (e.g. Budgam) also needs greater attention.     
 
Action Taken
 
State has decreased its OoSC from 377170 (2002-03) to 108560 (2006). Funds for various flexible strategies are being
provided under Alternative & Innovative Education Component of SSA. State has strategised to bring ST girls in to
KGBVs after bridging.
 
Recommendation/Observations

2.5.14  There appears to be a huge backlog in training teachers, an important component of SSA. The Committee
recommends that a detailed strategy should be chalked out for training the teachers in a time-bound manner and
development of curriculum and textbooks and training of teachers in English medium.
 
Action Taken
 
In J & K, teacher training needs are identified at the cluster level and are communicated to, collated and prioritized at
Zonal, District and State levels. State level as well as District level teacher training institutes (SIEs, DIETs) conduct
studies and reviews regarding teacher competence and area specific training needs. Based on zone specific and district
specific need assessment, ZRCs and DRGs have the freedom to adapt the training programmes to suit local needs and
circumstances.  
 
During 2006–07, the training was conducted exclusively in a trainee-active mode with least scope for lectures. Training
methods pursued included:
•         Group discussion & group work
•         Individual assignments
•         Presentation of good practices
•         Development of TLM
MHRD and Pedagogy Unit (TSG), in collaboration with Rajiv Gandhi Foundation in 2006 – 07 carried out series of
workshops for overall quality improvement in the State.
Sarva Shiksha Abhiyan (SSA) recognizes the critical role of teachers and to focus on their development needs, a number
of Block Resource Centres and Cluster Resource Centres have been set up. In-service training of teachers of 20-day
duration is organized each year. During 2006-07, a total of more than 23.57 lakh teachers were imparted 20-day training
upto 31.12.2006. In addition, over 1.39 lakh teachers were given Induction Training upto December 2006. Also, over 1.21
lakh untrained teachers were trained upto December 2006.  The content of in-service teacher training is decided by States,
and includes training in teaching English, as per needs.  NCERT is supporting States in reviewing their curriculum and
syllabi in the light of the National Curriculum Framework (NCF), 2005. 
 
Recommendation/Observations
 
2.5.15  The Committee recommends that efforts be made to see that the installments of SSA were not delayed and there
should be regular consultation in this regard between the Union and the State Government.
 
Action Taken
 
The instalments get delayed due to non-submission of UCs by the State’s SSA Implementation Society. However, to
improve fund flow this year (2007-08) ad-hoc grant of Rs.30 crore is under release.
 
Recommendation/Observations
 
2.5.16  The Committee found that in many schools in rural areas, the schools were functioning from temporary or semi-
permanent structures. Construction of permanent classrooms was one of the major problems that needed urgent attention.
The Committee, therefore, calls upon the Government to chalk out a contingency plan to construct permanent school
buildings wherever required in a fixed time schedule. The Government of India should give all possible help to the
Government of J&K for the construction of school buildings.
 
Action Taken
 
SSA is providing all support to J&K as per its norms for filling of the infrastructure gaps.    During the appraisal of AWP
& B and Project Approval Board, timelines for completion of pending works is drawn up.
 
Recommendation/Observations
 
2.5.18  The Committee is happy to see that the situation in J&K appears to have been improving and the Government

2.5.19  The Committee is fully aware of the ground situations prevailing in the State of J&K.  Education can be an
effective tool to eliminate militancy.  Keeping this in view, the Committee recommends that the Government of India
should time the release of funds according to the climatic and other conditions of the State. Giving all the benefits of
special category States that are available to NE States, must be considered for the J&K also. If need be, the guidelines of
SSA be amended in such a way so as to suit the ground realities, topography and other conditions of the State.
 
Action Taken
 
The framework for implementation of SSA is not an area specific document but is applicable throughout India. However,
it enjoys enough flexibility for local specific interventions. For e.g., the Annual Work Plan & Budget for SSA, are drawn
up by each district, so as to reflect local needs & priorities.  Though there has to be a conformity to the broad framework
of SSA, yet in norms for civil works, girls education, alternative education centres/ interventions, needs of children with
special needs, training of teachers etc. to name a few, local factors in funding norms are taken into regard.  There is also an
untied innovation fund amounting to Rs. 50 Lakh per district for meeting local specific needs.  The representatives of LEH
& Kargil Development Councils are represented in the Executive Committee & General Council of the State SSA
programme, which are empowered to notify norms relevant to different regions of the State.  Therefore, it is this
relationship which needs to be active so as to contextualize SSA for Leh & Kargil.
 
GOIs efforts are always to release State Government funds on time, but if States fail to clear their Utilization Certificates
which are due or fail to meet their State Share in a timely manner, then it becomes a cause for delay in releasing the next
instalment of Central Share.
 
Recommendation/Observations
 
2.5.20  The Committee feels that LADC being an elected body of the local people, is more close to and conversant with
the needs of the Leh and Ladakh regions. The Committee, therefore, recommends that the Government of India and
Government of J&K must involve and consult the LADC in implementing SSA keeping in view the fact that community
participation was the bedrock of this mission-mode programme. They may also be involved in formulating educational
curriculum specific to the different areas within the Leh and Ladakh regions. The Leh and Ladakh conditions must be kept
uppermost while laying own guidelines of SSA and other such schemes. The Government of India must bring out
necessary changes in the guidelines of Central/Centrally Sponsored Schemes to suit the conditions of these regions.

V.        IMPLEMENTATION OF SSA IN NORTH EASTERN STATES
 
Recommendation/Observations
 
5.1       The Committee discussed this issue with State Government officials from the North Eastern States and visited
schools in Assam, Manipur and Arunachal Pradesh.  The Committee found that all the States in the North East had begun
the SSA after some initial reluctance.  The expenditure figures showed very encouraging trend in this regard.  For example
while Assam spent 90 per cent of funds allocated in 2004-05, Nagaland spent 90.5 per cent, Mizoram 94 per cent and
Tripura spent as high as 99.8 per cent of the allocation.  Utilization of funds by Sikkim was 63 per cent, Meghalaya 60 per
cent, Manipur 65 per cent and Arunachal Pradesh around 55 per cent.  Main problem faced by NE States the Committee
found, was in providing their share.  All of them have severe financial constraints of their own.  The Committee was
informed that recently it was decided not to revise the sharing pattern of 75:25 as such, between the Center and the States. 
To tide over the financial difficulties of the North Eastern States, however 15 per cent of their share, as a special case, was
decided to be made available from the non-lapsable funds of the Ministry of Development of North Eastern Region
(DONER).  As a result, effectively, this share has since become 90:10 between Centre and NE States.
 
Action Taken
 
Noted.
 
Recommendation/Observations
 
5.2       The Committee welcomes this decision of the Central Government and hopes that the NE States would utilize this
opportunity to implement the programme with renewed vigour.  Regarding future requirements of funds, the States should
mobilize their own resources to fund the State share.
 
Action Taken
 
Noted.

Recommendation/Observations
 
5.4.4    The representatives of the Government of Nagaland submitted the following suggestions before the Committee:
(i) The State of Nagaland does not have a big revenue base. The predominant part of the state expenditure is financed with
the help of grants and other releases from the Government of India.  It becomes very difficult for the state to provide
adequate and enough funds for the various time bound social sector programmes. For proper and timely implementation of
the SSA programme, the funding pattern should be revised from 75:25 to 90:10. This may be especially considered for the
north eastern states as their internal revenue base is too small. For such a comprehensive and time bound programme, it is
essential that there are no problems in getting the required funds in time.
(ii)        The honorarium for teachers training may be increased to Rs.100 per day from the present Rs.70 per day.
(iii)       Rs.6.00 lakhs provided for establishing an Educational Block Resource Centre (EBRC) under SSA is insufficient
for carrying out the construction due to hilly and difficult terrain in remote areas of the State.  A higher amount, therefore,
is needed to meet construction costs of an EBRC.

Noted.

per the approved financial norms of the scheme.  Supplementary nutrition was being provided by the States out of their
own resources.  As some of the States were finding it difficult to meet this obligation, it has been decided to provide grant-
in-aid to States/UTs to the extent of 50% of the financial norms for supplementary nutrition or 50% of the actual
expenditure incurred, whichever is less, from the year 2005-06.
The Ministry is seized of the problem and the suggestion of the Committee shall be examined, subject to the availability of
funds.
